speaker: Siddhi Krishna (UC Berkeley)
title: Taut foliations dual to flows in Dehn surgeries
abstract: Taut foliations are an important and historically significant structure on 3-manifolds.The modern L-space conjecture makes a prediction about which rational homology spheres can admit a taut foliation. But where could the predicted taut foliations "come from"? Must they be compatible with “natural” geometric structures on the 3-manifold? In this talk, I'll discuss forthcoming work with John Baldwin and Matt Hedden, where we address a type of geography problem for taut foliations. We show -- in the sharpest possible way -- that when K is a fibered strongly quasipositive knot, large surgeries along K can never admit a taut foliation which is ‘’compatible’’ with the natural flow on the Dehn surgered manifold. I'll explain why this is surprising, and if time permits, sketch the proof. Expertise in the theories of foliations, flows, or Floer homology will be not assumed, all are welcome!

speaker: Samanda Zhang (University of Chicago)
title: Action of derived local-at-p Hecke algebra on cohomology of modular curve
abstract: In recent years, there has been growing interests in using derived enhancements in understanding structures/phenomena in the Langlands programme.  Such leads to interest in studying derived Hecke algebra and its action (e.g. Venkatesh, Schneider, etc.) Contrary to Venkatesh, which is a more global approach, we are interested in local information. Specifically,  using Emerton’s completed cohomology, we will give a canonical action of Schneider’s differential-graded (DG) Hecke algebra on cohomology of modular curve. As this DG algebra is much larger than the classical Hecke algebra, meaning there is additional information in its action,  we will explain some general methods in analyzing this DG-action and how one can use such additional DG structure. Surprisingly, this purely local derived structure gives us global Galois-theoretic information.

speaker: Tan Özalp (University of Notre Dame)
title: Canonical equivalence relations on $\mathrm{FIN}^{[\infty]}_2$
abstract: Erdos and Rado (1950) initiated canonical Ramsey theory by canonizing arbitrary equivalence relations on $[\omega]^n$ via the projection relations $\pi_I$ for $I \subseteq n$, meaning that any equivalence relation on $[\omega]^n$ has a restriction that agrees with some $\pi_I$. This was extended to equivalence relations on fronts of the natural numbers by Pudlák and Rödl (1982), and later to Borel relations on $[\omega]^{\omega}$ by Prömel and Voigt (1985). In parallel work, Taylor (1976) isolated five canonical equivalence relations on $\mathrm{FIN}$, and showed that any relation on $\mathrm{FIN}$ restricts to a canonical one. This was then generalized to arbitrary finite dimensions $\mathrm{FIN}^{[n]}$ by Lefmann (1996), and to Borel relations on $\mathrm{FIN}^{[\infty]}$ by Klein and Spinas (2005). Lopez-Abad (2007) generalized Taylor's result by canonizing the equivalence relations on $\mathrm{FIN}_k$ for every $k \geq 1$. However, higher dimensional canonization results for $\mathrm{FIN}_k$ were previously unknown. We develop an extension of the separating--mixing method of Prömel and Voigt (1985) to prove new canonization theorems for the equivalence relations on fronts of the Ramsey space $\mathrm{FIN}^{[\infty]}_2$, as well as for the Borel relations on the space. In particular, we give a complete list of the canonical equivalence relations on $\mathrm{FIN}^{[n]}_2$, and calculate their exact number in terms of $n$. These answer a question of Todorcevic.

speaker: Shashank Sule (UCLA)
title: Quantifying memorization in diffusion models
abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, i.e the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed in [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is bounded by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.

speaker: Yuchen Wu (UCSD)
title: Motivic stable stems of fields and number rings
abstract:
For any commutative ring $R$, the motivic stable homotopy groups (or motivic stable stems) $\pi_{**}(1_R)$ are an intricate mixture of the classical stable homotopy groups and the arithmetic of $R$ itself. Recently, using Galois approximation methods, Bachmann--Burklund--Xu made major progress in determining these groups, leading to a theoretical description of the $(\ell,\eta)$-completed motivic stable stems of all fields $k$ with $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq \ell$ for every odd prime $\ell$, and at $\ell = 2$ for all such fields containing a square root of $-1$, together with an efficient method for computing the motivic stable stems of all finite fields from those of $\mathbb{C}$.

In this talk I will survey these results, and discuss work in progress towards two extensions: a theoretical description of the motivic stable stems of all fields $k$ with $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq 2$ at the prime $2$, including those without a square root of $-1$, and a categorical assembly theorem which leads to an effective method for computing the motivic stable stems of all local/global fields and their rings of integers from those of $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{R}$, illustrated by explicit examples.

speaker: Molei Tao (Georgia Tech)
title: Understanding and enhancing diffusion models: a quantification of continuous diffusion model's creativity, and a provably scalable test-time scaling method for masked diffusion language models
abstract:
This talk will report two quantitative results, both centered around diffusion models' performance.

First, I will quantify the generalization capability of the classical diffusion model, i.e. the one for Euclidean data. The question is, when the generative model is not memorizing the training data, what new samples will it generate? This question is not only pertinent to privacy and copyright considerations, but also important for understanding whether/how diffusion model creates new knowledge. The inductive bias of diffusion model’s generation will be examined, leading to a quantification of how diffusion model generalizes. This quantification is the first result purely based on the empirical distribution without relying on any intangible population limit.

Then I will switch gear and describe the first test-time-scaling method for diffusion language models that provably converges to a reward tilted distribution in polynomial complexity of sequence length. The method, MDM-VGB, is a discrete diffusion sampler that augments unmasking generation with principled reward-guided remasking. It is based on a Markov Chain that is carefully designed to ensure fast mixing, and consequently good scalability. Cases where there is advantage over autoregressive language models will also be described.

speaker: Benjamin Bowman (AWS)
title: Priming: Hybrid State Space Models From Pre-trained Transformers
abstract:
Hybrid State-Space models combine Attention with recurrent State-Space
Model (SSM) layers, balancing eidetic memory from Attention with
compressed fading memory from SSMs. This yields smaller Key-Value
caches and faster decoding than Transformers, along with a richer
architectural design space. Exploring that design space at scale has
so far required training from scratch, a barrier that has kept most
large-model Hybrid research within a narrow range of architectures. We
introduce Priming, a method that turns Hybrid architecture design from
a pre-training problem into a knowledge transfer one. Priming
initializes a Hybrid model from a pre-trained Transformer and, through
short alignment and post-training phases, recovers downstream quality
using less than 0.5% of the source model's pre-training token budget.
Priming is agnostic to the source Transformer family (e.g., Qwen,
Llama, Mistral), model class (dense or Mixture-of-Experts), and model
scale. Priming enables us to run the first controlled comparison of
SSM layer types at scale under identical conditions. We evaluate,
Gated KalmaNet (GKA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN), and Mamba-2, and show that
their expressiveness hierarchy, GKA>GDN>Mamba-2, directly predicts
downstream performance on long-context reasoning tasks. We scale
Priming to 8B/32B reasoning models with native 128K contexts. Our
Hybrid GKA 32B improves over its source Qwen3-32B by +3.8 average
reasoning points, while staying within 1% of a Transformer
post-trained on the same data and enabling up to 2.3x higher decode
throughput. To foster research on Hybrid architectures, we release a
model zoo of primed Hybrid models for long-context reasoning and
instruction following, together with the Priming training and
inference code (Sequence Parallelism algorithms for long-context
training, optimized GKA kernels, and vLLM serving plugin), all under
Apache~2.0 License.

speaker: Moritz Voss (UCLA)
title: On a generalized Obizhaeva–Wang model with small instantaneous costs
abstract:
The Obizhaeva–Wang model (2005) is a cornerstone of financial mathematics for modeling price impact, the effect of trades on market prices, and plays a central role in optimal order execution and the study of market liquidity. In this talk, we present a novel approach to solving the associated singular stochastic control problem in a generalized framework. We also discuss the asymptotic behavior of a regularized version of the problem.

The talk is based on joint work with Marcel Nutz (Columbia University).

speaker: Ariana Chin (UCLA)
title: Zamolodchikov periodic cluster algebras: the Zamolodchikov fan
abstract: Zamolodchikov periodicity is a property of certain discrete dynamical systems and was one of the primary motivations for the creation of cluster algebras. In this talk, we discuss the classification of all Zamolodchikov periodic cluster algebras, with connections to W-graphs, root systems, and maximal green sequences. We introduce a natural red-blue statistic on the dynamical system that is homomesic, and use laminations to give a combinatorial proof of this result. In the process, we introduce the Zamolodchikov fan, which we believe to be of independent interest, and which is related to the positive tropical Grassmannian and the mutation fan.

speaker: Allen Lin
title: Boolean Functions, Arrow's Impossibility Theorem, and Sharp Thresholds
abstract: Arrow's impossibility theorem states that the only voting scheme that satisfies unanimity and independence of irrelevant alternatives is a dictatorship. Seemingly unrelatedly, random graphs exhibit a sharp dichotomy between being connected and disconnected as the edge probability varies over a short transition. We will connect the two using Boolean functions, functions that map n-bit binary strings of 0s and 1s to 0 or 1, and discuss how they can be used to model voting schemes and graph properties (e.g., connectedness). Then we will explore how influence (random changes in the bits) can be used to prove Arrow's theorem and the sharp threshold phenomena.

speaker: Will Feldman (Utah)
title: Perron extremal solutions of the Bernoulli one-phase problem (Joint with Caltech)
abstract: I will give some background about various notions of solution of the Bernoulli one-phase problem, their history, interest and connections. Then I will talk in more detail about the Perron extremal solutions. We show that the Perron solutions are also variational solutions and have some additional energetic structure. This allows the first analysis of the fine structure of the free boundary for Perron solutions in $d=2$. This is a joint work with Kerrek Stinson (Utah) and Farhan Abedin (Lafayette College).

speaker: Lars Becker (Princeton)
title: On the triangular Hilbert transform
abstract: The triangular Hilbert transform is a bilinear singular integral operator whose boundedness is known to imply several landmark results in harmonic analysis, including Carleson's theorem on pointwise convergence of Fourier series and uniform bounds for the bilinear Hilbert transform. OpenAI recently announced a proof of its boundedness. This talk discusses their proof, along with background and various extensions that are missing from their announcement.

speaker: Yanyu Wang (Vanderbilt University)
title: Free products and weak amenability
abstract: We will discuss some recent results on weak amenability for groups and von Neumann algebras, with an emphasis on free products.
